newsitem.title: UK: EMU debate sows confusion, but prices show resolve.
newsitem.headline: EMU debate sows confusion, but prices show resolve.

text.p: The debate about a postponement of European monetary union has shifted up a gear but actual prices in financial markets do not seem to be telling the same story, analysts said.

The relative stability of core European debt and currency markets like France and Belgium and the weakness this week in German government bond prices seem inconsistent with heightened concerns about a generalised delay to the EMU start date of January 1, 1999.
"The market still basically believes in a narrow EMU going ahead," said Peter Von Maydell, currency economist at UBS.
French markets would, arguably, suffer heavily if EMU were derailed but have barely flinched in recent weeks and months.
German Bund prices, meantime, have traditionally acted as a safe-haven from the volatility associated with EMU uncertainty. Yet, this week they even underperformed neighbouring markets.

One explanation is the bulk of investors remain confident of EMU going ahead among a narrow group of countries on time in 1999. Another is that non-European investors are no longer discriminating between European markets and may abandon Europe as a bloc until more details of the euro launch emerge next year.
The claim and counter-claim and ebb and flow of opinion is just becoming confusing and ultimately fruitless, some argue.

"Investors will probably do best to ignore the clamour of official pronouncements regarding the EMU project," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking. One problem is that many politicians and central bankers have their own agendas and have an interest in influencing market sentiment, he said.

"Investors would be better advised to watch political developments in the two key EU member states of France and Germany," said Lewis. "Only if the leaders in these countries remain firmly committed to monetary union will EMU have any chance of going ahead, in any shape or form, in January 1999."
Yet concern about a Far East boycott of Europe has surfaced just as the Japanese start their new fiscal year next month.
Last week, Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong monetary authority, said the body has reduced the proportion of European exposure in its investments.

"We do not know what is going on with European currency union. Only after the euro is firmly established can we be sure," said Yam. "In the meantime, if we want to manage our risk, we have to reduce our exposure to Europe."
Analysts said this could be a bigger trend.

"There's some question about whether the mark really is a safe haven and whether in fact all of Europe is not one big problem which investors are not particularly happy being exposed to," said Robert Hayward, economist at Bank of America.

Yet, belief in a narrow group of countries - about six to eight - starting monetary union on time is hard to shake despite concerns that German economic sluggishness makes it difficult for it to satisfy the budgetary and debt entry goals.

To the chagrin of Bund investors, there have been signs Germany may well take part in EMU in 1999 by making full use of the flexible wording contained in the Maastricht Treaty's rules on public debt and budget deficit levels.

The reference target for budget deficits is three percent of a country's annual output and debt levels should be under 60 percent of output. However, the Treaty states special circumstances can be taken into account if deficit and debt levels are close to these levels and deemed to be sustainable.

German finance minister Theo Waigel alluded to this flexibility at a EU finance ministers meeting on Monday when he argued that special circumstances like German reunification and high German net contributions to the EU had inflated its debt.

European Monetary Institute president Alexandre Lamfalussy, several Bundesbank members and even the German Social Democrat leader Oskar Lafontaine have this month stressed the flexibility of the Treaty's rules once sustainability is accepted.

The constant stress on sustainability is also partly why Italian, Spanish and Swedish markets are suffering most from the recent debate, said analysts. Market players still believe it is most likely that these countries will not be allowed to start EMU with the core.
Meantime, there is still no sign of any capital disturbance within the core European markets like France and the Benelux.
The mark/French franc rate, seen as the linchpin of EMU, has not budged from a 1.5 centime range for four months and one-year implied volatility in the options market is just 2.2 percent.

Some argue French fundamentals justify this stability regardless of EMU considerations, but few analysts say there is no risk to the current French monetary and fiscal policy mix if the EMU discipline were removed.
"It's hard to believe that the perceived risk in French markets is identical with or without EMU," said one senior trader at a Swiss bank here.
